statement: In randomized trials of people with chronic pain, mostly neuropathic or cancer pain (28 trials, 2,454 participants; 17 at high and 9 at unclear risk of bias), cannabinoid medicines compared with placebo, in trials with follow-up of at most 15 weeks, are associated with a small reduction in pain. Nabiximols (a THC and CBD spray used in the mouth) was the commonest product (13 of the 28 trials) and nearly all of the pooled trials tested it. In a 2015 meta-analysis of the parallel-group trials (Whiting et al., 2015; AMSTAR 2 critically low), 37% of people on cannabinoids and 31% on placebo had their pain reduced by at least 30% (254 of 685 against 215 of 685, the crude totals of the 8 trials in the review's forest plot; about 6 more in 100, editors' arithmetic), an odds ratio of 1.41 (95% CI 0.99 to 2.00; 8 trials, 7 of them of nabiximols and 1 of smoked THC, 1,370 people; I2 48%) that does not exclude no difference; the 7 nabiximols trials alone gave 1.32 (0.94 to 1.86), and the one smoked-THC trial, of 50 people, the largest effect (OR 3.43, 1.03 to 11.48). Pain on a 0 to 10 scale was 0.46 points lower with nabiximols (95% CI 0.11 to 0.80 lower; 6 trials, 948 people; I2 59%); the review team rated both outcomes moderate certainty and names no threshold for a clinically important change. More people rated themselves improved overall (OR 2.08, 1.21 to 3.59; 6 trials, 267 people; low certainty by the review team), neuropathic-pain scale scores were 3.89 points lower on a 0 to 100 scale (0.47 to 7.32 lower), and the Brief Pain Inventory (-0.17, -0.50 to 0.16) and quality of life (EQ-5D, -0.01, -0.05 to 0.02) did not differ. The review concludes that moderate-quality evidence supports cannabinoids for chronic pain, which its Discussion narrows to neuropathic or cancer pain treated with smoked THC or nabiximols, but the outcomes so rated are either not statistically significant or small. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: In trials of up to 15 weeks, people with long-lasting pain who took a cannabis medicine (in the combined trials, nearly always a THC and CBD mouth spray) scored their pain about half a point lower on a 0 to 10 scale than people who took a dummy medicine (placebo). About 37 in 100 people on the medicine and 31 in 100 on the dummy had their pain cut by at least 30%, a difference that could be due to chance. Most trials had weaknesses in how they were run or reported.
population: People with chronic pain (mostly neuropathic pain; also cancer pain, diabetic neuropathy, fibromyalgia, HIV neuropathy and others) in randomized trials published up to April 2015; ages are not reported in the review's main text
exposure: Cannabinoid medicines as given in the trials: nabiximols (oromucosal THC and CBD spray) in 13 of the 28 trials and in nearly all pooled ones, also smoked THC, nabilone, THC spray, dronabinol, vaporized cannabis and others; doses are study conditions
outcome: At least 30% pain reduction; pain on 0 to 10 numerical rating scales; Brief Pain Inventory; Neuropathic Pain Scale; patients' global impression of change; quality of life (EQ-5D)
magnitude: Whiting et al. 2015, parallel-group trials, random effects, cannabinoid against placebo: at least 30% pain reduction 37% vs 31% (254/685 vs 215/685, crude totals in the review's Figure 2; about 6 more in 100, editors' arithmetic), OR 1.41 (95% CI 0.99 to 2.00; 8 trials, 1,370 patients; I2 48%; GRADE moderate by the review team); the 7 nabiximols trials alone OR 1.32 (0.94 to 1.86); smoked-THC trial OR 3.43 (1.03 to 11.48; 50 patients); in Figure 2, 5 of the 8 trials favour cannabinoids (3 significantly) and 3 favour placebo (none significantly); neuropathic pain OR 1.38 (0.93 to 2.03; 6 trials); nabiximols: 0 to 10 pain scale WMD -0.46 (-0.80 to -0.11; 6 trials, 948 patients; I2 59%; moderate); Brief Pain Inventory -0.17 (-0.50 to 0.16; 3 trials); Neuropathic Pain Scale -3.89 on 0 to 100 (-7.32 to -0.47; 5 trials); global impression of change OR 2.08 (1.21 to 3.59; 6 trials, 267 patients; I2 68%; low); EQ-5D -0.01 (-0.05 to 0.02; 3 trials).

evidence.extracted: Chronic pain: 28 studies (63 reports; 2454 participants), mostly neuropathic pain (12), also cancer pain, diabetic neuropathy, fibromyalgia, HIV neuropathy and others; 13 nabiximols, 4 smoked THC, 5 nabilone, 3 THC spray, 2 dronabinol, 1 vaporized cannabis, 1 ajulemic acid and 1 oral THC (30 products for 28 studies, unexplained); all placebo-controlled except one against amitriptyline; risk of bias low in 2, unclear in 9, high in 17.

Nabiximols: pain NRS WMD -0.46 (-0.80 to -0.11) on 0 to 10, 6 trials, 948 patients, I2 59%, moderate; Brief Pain Inventory -0.17 (-0.50 to 0.16), 3 trials; Neuropathic Pain Scale -3.89 (-7.32 to -0.47) on 0 to 100, 5 trials; global impression of change OR 2.08 (1.21 to 3.59), 6 trials (5 nabiximols and 1 nabilone by Table 2; the text names nabiximols), 267 patients, I2 68%, low; EQ-5D -0.01 (-0.05 to 0.02), 3 trials. Sensitivity analyses adding crossover trials were reported as consistent. The abstract's percentages are not derived in the text or tables; they equal the crude event totals of Figure 2 (see the Figure 2 anchor); the cancer-pain subgroup estimate is misprinted and not used.

evidence.extracted: Figure 2: 254 of 685 people with cannabinoids and 215 of 685 with placebo had at least 30% less pain across the 8 trials (37.1% and 31.4%, the abstract's 37% and 31%; editors' arithmetic), OR 1.41 (0.99 to 2.00), I2 47.6%; smoked THC (Abrams 2007) 13 of 25 against 6 of 25, OR 3.43 (1.03 to 11.48); the 7 nabiximols trials together 241 of 660 against 209 of 660, OR 1.32 (0.94 to 1.86), I2 44.5%. Five of the 8 trials favour cannabinoids (3 significantly: Abrams 2007, Johnson 2010, Serpell 2014) and 3 favour placebo, none significantly (GW Pharmaceuticals 2005, Portenoy 2012, Selvarajah 2010). The heterogeneity P values are printed malformed, as .0.64 and .0.94; recomputed from the I2 values and the number of trials they are about .064 and .094 (editors' calculation), probably the intended values. The Discussion places the moderate-quality evidence in chronic neuropathic or cancer pain (smoked THC and nabiximols).

risk_of_bias.note: Of the 28 pain trials, 17 at high and 9 at unclear risk of bias; across the review, withdrawals were often not handled and only 57% reported adequate blinding of participants, while psychoactive effects (euphoria and dizziness several times more frequent with cannabinoids in the review's adverse-event data) can reveal who had the active drug (card sc_whiting_2015).

inconsistency.note: I2 48% and 59%: moderate heterogeneity. In the responder pool 5 of the 8 trials point towards benefit and 3 towards placebo, none of those 3 significantly (Figure 2), and the review says the continuous results were not consistent across trials; not rated down, because the intervals overlap and the pooled estimates point the same way, but a stricter reading could rate down here.

indirectness.note: Worded for short trials of mostly pharmaceutical products in people with chronic pain; it does not extend to herbal cannabis as most people use it or to long-term use.

imprecision.note: The responder estimate (0.99 to 2.00) includes no difference; the pain-scale difference is precise but small, its whole interval under 1 point on a 10-point scale.

publication_bias.note: Not investigated by the review, which used trial-registry records; many nabiximols trials were registered by the manufacturer, and trial funding is not reported; not downgraded separately.

grade.reasoning: Randomized trials start high; down one for risk of bias and one for imprecision: low. The review team rated these outcomes moderate; the editors also rate down for imprecision, because the outcome that matters most to patients (at least 30% less pain) does not exclude no effect, and the pain-scale reduction, though precise, is small. The largest responder effect comes from the one smoked-THC trial of 50 people; the 7 nabiximols trials alone give OR 1.32 (0.94 to 1.86). Status replicated: 5 of the 8 responder trials point the same way (3 significantly), with moderate heterogeneity and 3 trials pointing towards placebo without significance (Figure 2, viewed at adjudication); the pain-scale pool has 6 trials whose individual results the article does not show.
